title: Hypertrophy Q&A #1
summary: First hypertrophy Q&A. NH tells a chronically overtrained intermediate to stop chasing strength numbers and get tonnage from accessories with a more specific upper/lower split, advises an 18-year-old rugby player against forcing weight gain, and covers forearm training, squat/deadlift carryover, when push-ups stop being enough, and rings for hypertrophy.
claims: Hypertrophy Q&As will be posted monthly; questions must go under the matching Q&A video or they get lost
Most people who think they are overtraining are right: they answer regression by adding more volume, which deepens the regression
Feeling futile in sessions, fearing declines and juggling strength gains against accessory volume are signs of too much focus on strength progression for a hypertrophy goal
Get stronger because bigger numbers feed more tonnage, and most tonnage trickles down into variations and accessories, not the strength work
Detach emotionally from main-lift numbers; a pure squat stalling for three months is fine if other knee-flexion lifts progress
Check what share of each session's tonnage comes from the first heavy strength exercise; if most of it does, rethink the program because a plateau there bleeds all progress dry
Online strength standards are unreliable: mostly unverified self-reported polls or powerlifter data, irrelevant to someone not training for powerlifting
A 180 lb lifter benching 230 has enough strength to grow a lot by accumulating volume on variations with 180-190 lb
Some lifters have high in-session work capacity but poor between-session recovery; full body fails them because they destroy everything and cannot repeat it three days later
For high work capacity / poor recovery lifters: avoid the extra volume that causes overtraining, use more specific splits and raise frequency so each body part gets days to recover alone
Splitting a full-body session's muscles over several days takes the same total time but recovers better because each muscle gets a dedicated day plus lighter days
Use upper/lower as a template but be selective inside it: do not put chest and upper back on the same upper day; e.g. chest-triceps-shoulders, minimizing muscles hit to maximize frequency
Deliberately maintain the strength work and trigger a controlled plateau at constant tonnage, then build volume and variations around it
Gaining 25 lb by next season at 18 years old will not be muscle; forcing a goal weight for a sport usually backfires
Athletes doing strength training should test sprint speed and agility drills regularly to detect regressions and weigh them against strength gains
Off-season athletes should focus on hypertrophy but keep testing athletic performance; in season they should still keep 2-3 hours a week of gym work rather than going all-or-nothing
When I played football, guys chasing a target weight at all cost always backfired
5x20 forearm curls and extensions is a nucleus-overload style scheme and would grow forearms
Forearms may be a poor target for daily nucleus overload because tired forearms hurt curls and pulls where you do not use straps; every workout is OK only if training about 3x/week
High-volume wrist extensions often cause wrist pain and risk tendinitis
Superset wrist curls with a horizontal press or squat instead of leaving them for the end, where they get skipped
Strapless deadlifts work the forearm isometrically, mostly the top of the forearm, but are mainly a grip exercise and pure grip work is not the best for forearm size
Get as much forearm work as possible from double-overhand deadlifts, then switch to straps when the grip fails; still isolate the forearms
Many huge deadlifters like Pete Rubish and an 800-900 lb puller have thin forearms; the deadlift is a posterior chain lift, not a forearm exercise
The more specific the accessory the better; the best squat accessory is the pause squat, which builds strength in the hole and confidence
The best deadlift accessory is more deadlifting: after the heavy top set, 4x3 with a weight you can comfortably triple
Good mornings are an underrated squat builder; a box squat with the safety squat bar works well for the deadlift
For novices push-ups are as effective as dips or an empty-bar bench because they are intense; as you progress loaded presses win because push-ups cannot be loaded
High-rep push-ups end from systemic failure, pump discomfort or a weak link like triceps rather than chest failure
Weighted push-ups are less practical than dips or bench because they are hard to load alone
Keep doing push-ups as an advanced lifter by placing them at the end of a press day so fatigue pushes them into an effective intensity range
Example: after heavy pressing push-ups go 35, 29, 21 reps; fresh they would be 45-50, 48, 46 and do little damage
Push-ups are underrated for chest development because hand width can be varied
Technicality-to-hypertrophy ratio: some lifts grow muscle but take too much skill time to be worth it, and rings are one of them
Gymnasts get big biceps by being elite at rings from childhood; copying their training will not give you their arms
Rings are easy on the wrists, adjustable and easy to learn; scaled gymnastics movements on rings are good hypertrophy work with more stabilizer involvement
Ring push-ups are harder and better for chest than push-ups thanks to deeper stretch and free wrist/elbow angles
Rings are the main way to do bodyweight horizontal pulls, which are underrated
exercises: builds strength where you need it and confidence out of the bottom
4x3 with a comfortable triple weight after the top set
best deadlift builder is more deadlifting
safety squat bar, Westside-style box squat
carryover to the deadlift via back angle and hip height
switch to straps when grip fails
place at end of press day
fatigue makes them intense enough for advanced lifters
